metadata.name: Decision Mirror - Onboarding Quiz Gold Dataset
metadata.source_document: Decision Mirror Task 3 - Onboarding Quiz & Initial Labeled Dataset

time_horizon.name: Time Horizon
time_horizon.polarity: low = immediate benefit, high = delayed payoff

self_consistency.note: Not measured at onboarding; computed longitudinally.

notes: gold_value and answer text are copied verbatim from Task 3 and must not be modified.
The evidence rationale is written per trait and answer direction (Task 3 only gave one explicit example, Q01_A).
confidence = 0.70 per Task 3 Section 5 (item-level). Task 3 Section 7 example shows 0.9; this inconsistency should be resolved by the team.
situational_factor is null for all items; all items are marked trait_revealing.
This is an engineering calibration dataset, not a clinically validated one.

questions.scenario: You receive two job offers. Offer A is stable and pays $1,500/month. Offer B pays $1,000/month now but could grow substantially if the company succeeds.

options.text: I would choose the stable $1,500 offer.
I would probably choose the stable offer unless the startup had unusually strong evidence of success.
I would compare both carefully; the risk and upside are roughly equally important.
I would lean toward the startup because the upside is worth accepting some uncertainty.
I would choose the startup; uncertainty is acceptable when the potential upside is much larger.

questions.scenario: You have savings that could support you for several months. You can either keep them in a predictable low-return account or use part of them for a business idea with a meaningful chance of failure.

options.text: I would keep the money safe; preserving what I have matters most.
I would invest only a small amount because I strongly prefer protecting the savings.
I would split the money between safety and the opportunity.
I would invest a meaningful portion after checking the downside.
I would accept the possibility of losing much of it for a chance to build something much larger.

questions.scenario: A travel company offers a heavily discounted trip, but the destination has a higher-than-usual chance of disruption. A normal trip costs much more.

options.text: I would pay more for the reliable trip.
I would probably choose the reliable trip unless the disruption risk looked very small.
I would weigh the discount against the disruption risk equally.
I would take the discounted trip if the possible inconvenience were manageable.
I would take the discounted trip; I enjoy accepting uncertainty for a worthwhile benefit.

questions.scenario: You can choose a guaranteed moderate reward today or enter a fair competition with a substantial chance of receiving a much larger reward.

options.text: I would take the guaranteed reward.
I would usually take the guaranteed reward.
It would depend on how large the difference is.
I would usually take the competition for the larger upside.
I would strongly prefer the competition because the larger upside is worth the uncertainty.

questions.scenario: A new technology could make your current skillset much more valuable, but it could also make part of it obsolete. You have time to learn it without leaving your current path.

options.text: I would avoid depending on it until it becomes proven.
I would learn it cautiously while protecting my current path.
I would experiment while keeping both options open.
I would invest heavily in learning it because the upside is meaningful.
I would move aggressively toward it because I am comfortable betting on emerging opportunities.

questions.scenario: You can spend your free time earning extra money this month or spend that time learning a skill that may significantly improve your income several years from now.

options.text: I would take the money now; the immediate benefit matters most.
I would mostly take the money now, with some learning on the side.
I would split the time between both.
I would give most of the time to the skill for the future benefit.
I would prioritize the long-term skill almost entirely if the future payoff is credible.

questions.scenario: You can buy a cheaper product now or wait several months and save for a much better version that will last longer.

options.text: I would buy the cheaper one now.
I would lean toward buying now unless the better version is clearly worth waiting for.
I would compare the immediate usefulness with the long-term value.
I would wait if the long-term improvement is substantial.
I would willingly wait and sacrifice convenience now for the better long-term outcome.

questions.scenario: You are offered a course that requires six months of difficult study before providing a career benefit.

options.text: I would prefer something that produces a benefit quickly.
I would hesitate unless the benefit is fairly near.
I would consider both the effort now and the future payoff.
I would accept the short-term effort for a strong future opportunity.
I am comfortable making a major short-term sacrifice for a payoff several years away.

questions.scenario: You can solve a recurring problem with a quick temporary fix or spend more time now on a solution that is likely to prevent the problem for years.

options.text: I would take the quick fix.
I would usually take the quick fix unless the recurring cost is obvious.
I would balance the time saved now against the long-term benefit.
I would invest the extra time for a durable solution.
I would strongly prefer the durable solution even if it creates substantial work now.

questions.scenario: You receive a bonus. You can spend it on an experience this month or save it toward a major goal you want to reach in three years.

options.text: I would mostly spend it now.
I would spend most of it and save a little.
I would divide it between current enjoyment and the future goal.
I would save most of it for the goal.
I would prioritize the three-year goal and accept giving up most immediate enjoyment.

questions.scenario: You receive a career opportunity in another city. It is clearly better for your own career, but your partner strongly prefers staying where you are.

options.text: I would prioritize my partner's preference unless there were no alternative.
I would lean toward staying because the relationship's preference matters more.
I would treat my career and my partner's preference as equally important.
I would lean toward taking the opportunity if it strongly advances my career.
I would take it if it is the right move for me, even if my partner prefers otherwise.

questions.scenario: Your team must choose between an approach that makes your individual work easier and one that makes the overall team's work better but creates extra work for you.

options.text: I would choose the team-benefiting approach.
I would usually accept extra work if it clearly helps the team.
I would compare my workload with the team benefit.
I would favor the approach that makes my own work easier unless the team impact is large.
I would prioritize my own workload and goals unless helping the team is essential.

questions.scenario: You have one free weekend. You can use it for something personally important or help a family member with a project they asked you to join.

options.text: I would almost certainly help my family member.
I would lean toward helping them.
I would split the weekend or negotiate a compromise.
I would lean toward my own plans unless the request is important.
I would keep my weekend for my own priorities unless there is a serious reason to change them.

questions.scenario: You are offered a promotion that improves your career but requires you to give up a commitment that is important to a close group you belong to.

options.text: I would protect the group's commitment.
I would usually put the group commitment first.
I would seek a solution that protects both.
I would lean toward the promotion if it is important for my career.
I would prioritize the promotion and accept disappointing the group if necessary.

questions.scenario: You are choosing a place to live. One option is much better for your daily routine; another is better for the people you live with.

options.text: I would choose what best serves the people I live with.
I would lean toward their needs.
I would try to find the best compromise.
I would lean toward what works best for my own routine.
I would choose what best serves my own needs even if others prefer the alternative.

questions.scenario: You need to buy a laptop. Several models are good, and there is no urgent deadline.

options.text: I would research for a long time, compare many models and revisit the decision.
I would spend considerable time researching before committing.
I would research the main options and decide once I have enough information.
I would narrow it to a few options and decide fairly quickly.
I would pick one that seems right and commit quickly.

questions.scenario: You are choosing between two restaurants for a casual meal with no strong preference.

options.text: I would carefully compare menus, reviews and prices before deciding.
I would ask several people or compare reviews first.
I would look briefly and then decide.
I would choose one of the first reasonable options.
I would decide almost immediately based on my first instinct.

questions.scenario: You receive a non-urgent offer and have several days to respond.

options.text: I would use most of the available time researching and reconsidering.
I would deliberate substantially before responding.
I would think it through and respond once I felt sufficiently informed.
I would make a decision after a short review rather than using all the time.
I would probably decide quickly if my first impression were positive.

questions.scenario: You are choosing a course from several similar options.

options.text: I would build a detailed comparison and revisit it before choosing.
I would research extensively and possibly ask several people.
I would compare the main criteria and then choose.
I would select a strong option after a quick comparison.
I would choose the first course that feels like a good fit.

questions.scenario: You need to choose a small purchase today, and changing your mind later would be easy.

options.text: I would still research extensively before buying.
I would compare several options carefully.
I would check the basics and decide.
I would make a quick choice among reasonable options.
I would trust my first acceptable option and move on.

questions.scenario: Two apartments are similar. One has better numbers for price, commute and space; the other immediately feels like home.

options.text: I would choose the one that feels right even if the numbers are worse.
I would give my feeling more weight than the comparison.
I would balance the feeling with the measurable differences.
I would give the measurable differences more weight unless the feeling is unusually strong.
I would choose primarily from a structured comparison of price, commute, space and other criteria.

questions.scenario: You are deciding whether to accept an opportunity. Your gut strongly says yes, but the available data shows several meaningful disadvantages.

options.text: I would follow my gut despite the data.
I would give the gut feeling substantial weight.
I would investigate the conflict between feeling and evidence before deciding.
I would mostly follow the evidence unless the emotional signal reveals something concrete.
I would prioritize the evidence and explicit criteria over my gut feeling.

questions.scenario: You are buying an expensive device and have narrowed the choice to three options.

options.text: I would choose the one I connect with or simply like most.
I would let personal preference and feeling dominate the final choice.
I would combine how each feels with objective features.
I would use objective features as the main guide but still consider preference.
I would build a detailed comparison using specifications, price and performance.

questions.scenario: A friend recommends a decision because they have a strong positive feeling about it, but you have numerical evidence that points in another direction.

options.text: I would trust the feeling and recommendation.
I would give the personal judgment more weight than the numbers.
I would investigate both before choosing.
I would lean toward the numbers while considering why the friend feels strongly.
I would prioritize the quantitative evidence and explicit comparison.

questions.scenario: You must choose between two career paths. One feels exciting and meaningful; the other scores better across salary, stability and advancement criteria.

options.text: I would choose the exciting and meaningful path because that feeling matters most.
I would let meaning and excitement outweigh most of the criteria.
I would balance meaning with the objective career factors.
I would give the career criteria more weight while still considering meaning.
I would score the alternatives against explicit criteria and choose the stronger overall result.
